overview.text: Atoms are tiny building blocks of ordinary matter, and their structure helps identify elements and distinguish isotopes and ions. Each has a compact central nucleus containing positively charged protons and, in most atoms, neutral neutrons; negatively charged electrons occupy the space around it. An atom’s proton count, called its atomic number, determines its element. Atoms of the same element can have different neutron counts and thus be different isotopes. A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons, but gaining or losing electrons makes it electrically charged—an ion—without changing its proton-defined element. The nucleus is extremely small relative to the whole atom.

key_facts.text: Protons are positive, neutrons have no electric charge, and electrons are negative.
Protons and neutrons are in the nucleus; electrons are outside it.
The atomic number is the number of protons in an atom’s nucleus and identifies its element.
Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons; gaining or losing electrons forms an ion.
